theory.title: Presupposition and shared assumptions
theory.explanation: A presupposition is information a speaker presents as already accepted or recoverable from context. It often survives negation and questioning: “She stopped attending” and “She did not stop attending” both suggest prior attendance. Common triggers include factive verbs (regret, realise), change-of-state verbs (stop, resume), definite descriptions, iteratives (again), and focus particles (even). Presuppositions can be accommodated when listeners accept them without challenge, but accommodation is not proof that the assumption is true.
theory.tip: For each sentence, underline the trigger, state the presupposed proposition, then ask whether the context supports it.

patterns.label: Change of state
examples: They resumed negotiations. → Negotiations had taken place before.
She stopped publishing the figures. → She had published them before.

patterns.label: Factive predicates
examples: He regretted that he had resigned. → He had resigned.
They realised that the figures were wrong. → The figures were wrong.

patterns.label: Iteratives
examples: The system failed again. → It had failed before.

patterns.label: Focus particles
examples: Even the chair objected. → The chair's objection is presented as unexpected.

content.passage:
A city council notice announced that the authority would “resume its efforts to make the waterfront accessible”. The wording appeared innocuous, yet residents quickly asked when those efforts had first begun and why they had been interrupted. The verb “resume” quietly presents an earlier period of activity as established background; it does not, by itself, explain the interruption or establish who was responsible.

At the subsequent meeting, a councillor asked whether the authority would finally acknowledge that its previous plan had failed. The question carried more than a request for information. “Finally” suggested that an acknowledgement was overdue, while “failed” treated the plan's outcome as settled. The project team rejected both assumptions, noting that the plan had been suspended pending a safety review and had never been formally evaluated.

This exchange illustrates why presuppositions deserve scrutiny. They can make communication efficient by relying on shared knowledge, but they can also smuggle contested claims into apparently ordinary sentences. A careful respondent need not reject every background assumption; rather, they should distinguish what the wording takes for granted from what the available evidence actually supports.

items.prompt: Explain how a presupposition differs from an entailment.
items.modelAnswer: A presupposition is backgrounded information treated as given and may survive negation; an entailment is a necessary consequence of a proposition.

items.prompt: Analyse the hidden assumption in: “When will the department stop wasting public money?”
items.modelAnswer: The question presupposes that the department is wasting public money and that the behaviour should stop; neither premise is established by the question itself.

items.prompt: Give an example of a factive verb and explain the assumption it introduces.
items.modelAnswer: “She regretted cancelling the meeting” presupposes that the meeting was cancelled; regretted presents the embedded proposition as factive.

items.prompt: How can presuppositions make political rhetoric persuasive?
items.modelAnswer: They allow a speaker to package contested evaluations as shared background, reducing the likelihood that listeners will challenge them.

items.prompt: Respond diplomatically to: “Why did you ignore the warning?” when you dispute the premise.
items.modelAnswer: I would first clarify that I do not accept that I ignored it; I reviewed the warning and reached a different assessment of the risk.

items.prompt: Explain the pragmatic effect of “even” in a sentence of your choice.
items.modelAnswer: “Even the sceptics supported the proposal” frames the sceptics as an unexpected group to support it, making the support seem especially significant.

items.prompt: Discuss when shared assumptions improve communication and when they become risky.
items.modelAnswer: They improve efficiency when genuinely shared and relevant, but become risky when they conceal disagreement or encode unsupported claims.

items.prompt: Rewrite a loaded question as a neutral request for information.
items.modelAnswer: Instead of “When will you admit the plan failed?”, ask “How would you assess the plan's outcomes against its original objectives?”

items.prompt: Describe how a counterfactual can expose an unstated assumption.
items.modelAnswer: A counterfactual tests a premise by imagining a different condition, making dependencies and causal claims easier to examine.

items.prompt: Summarise the difference between challenging a premise and refusing to answer.
items.modelAnswer: Challenging a premise addresses the assumptions built into a question; it can be a substantive answer rather than an evasion.

content.audioTranscript: The interviewer asked when the committee would finally reconsider its decision. The chair replied that the question assumed the decision was irreversible, which it was not. She added that the review had resumed after new evidence emerged, although no conclusion had yet been reached.
